warmup.q: The bakery's order page builds a quote with Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount). The price and the delivery fee arrive, but this customer has no discount, so discount completes empty. What does the zip do?
options: It emits a tuple with null in the third slot
It completes empty, with no value and no error, and cancels the other calls
It waits forever for the discount
warmup.why: Mono.zip needs one value from every source. When one completes empty, there is nothing to put in that slot, so the zip completes empty right away and cancels the others. Reactive Streams forbids null items, so a tuple with a null slot can't happen. The quote quietly disappears, which is the trap this lesson fixes.

opening:
Picture the packing table at the end of the bakery, where two belts arrive. One brings loaves from the oven. The other brings jars of jam from the jam kitchen. The packer can work in four ways. She can box whatever arrives first, from either belt. She can finish all the loaves before she looks at the jam. She can make gift boxes, one loaf and one jar in each. Or she can keep the price board on the wall up to date, whenever either price changes.

Reactor has an operator for each of those four, and they differ in two things: when each belt is switched on, and when something comes out. The trap is the gift box. When one belt arrives empty, Reactor's gift-box packer ships no box and says nothing at all.

Transforming streams worked on one belt at a time. In this lesson, we'll join several: zip for gift boxes, merge and concat for mixing and taking turns, and combineLatest for the price board. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started at a packing table with two belts. zip makes gift boxes, and ships nothing when one belt is empty. merge boxes whatever comes first, concat finishes one belt before it switches on the next, and combineLatest keeps the price board current.

Now search your own code for Mono.zip( and check each source: what should happen if it completes empty?

Next, we'll look at errors, retries and timeouts. Every combinator here gave up at the first error, because onError is a terminal signal. When the icing machine fails once, how do we try again, and how long should we wait before giving up?

sections.h: Four ways to join two belts, starting with zip, which pairs by position
sections.html:
Every combining operator answers two questions: when does it subscribe to each source, and when does something come out? Here are the four from the opening in those terms. zip subscribes to all its sources at once and emits only when it has one item from each. merge subscribes to all at once and emits each item as it arrives. concat subscribes to the next source only after the previous one has completed. combineLatest subscribes to all at once and emits whenever any source changes. We'll take them in that order, starting with the gift boxes.

Flux.zip(a, b) waits until every source has emitted one item, combines those items, and repeats. It pairs by position, first with first and second with second, like one loaf and one jar in each gift box. It completes as soon as any source completes, so the extra items of a longer source are left over. Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")) gives [[1,a], [2,b]], and the 3 is never used.

In everyday code you'll use Mono.zip far more often, for fan-out: starting several independent calls at once and combining their results. The bakery's order page needs three lookups for a cake quote, each from a different part of the program:

Java
Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip(prices.forCake(cake), delivery.feeTo(address), tax.rateFor(address))
        .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3()));
Kotlin
val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip(prices.forCake(cake), delivery.feeTo(address), tax.rateFor(address))
    .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) }

Mono.zip subscribes to all of its sources at once. If the price takes 100 ms, the delivery fee 300 ms and the tax rate 200 ms, the quote is ready after 300 ms, not 600. The result is a tuple, a small object that holds one value per source, read with getT1(), getT2() and so on. There are typed versions for up to eight sources.

If any source fails, the zip fails and cancels the others. That's usually what you want. The surprise is the other ending. The Mono.zip Javadoc, Reactor's reference page for the method, says it plainly: an "empty completion of any source will cause other sources to be cancelled and the resulting Mono to immediately ... complete". No error, no value.

ZipDemo, in the Try it, zips a price, a delivery fee and a discount, for a customer who has no discount. So the discount Mono completes empty:

  price lookup cancelled
Mono.zip result: null

The price lookup was cancelled, and doOnSuccess received null, which here means "completed empty". No quote, no error, no complaint. One belt arrived empty, so the quiet packer shipped no box. A web page would show an empty answer, block() would return null, and the logs would show nothing at all.

This is where the gift-box picture breaks. A real packer with no jam would say "we're out of jam". Mono.zip just completes. So decide what "empty" means for each source, and say it in code. Either it has a sensible default, as a missing discount means no discount, or it's a real error, as a cake must have a price:

Java
Mono<BigDecimal> safeDiscount = discount.defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO);   // empty means "no discount"
Mono<BigDecimal> safePrice = price.switchIfEmpty(
        Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException("missing price")));      // empty is an error
Kotlin
val safeDiscount = discount.defaultIfEmpty(BigDecimal.ZERO)                  // empty means "no discount"
val safePrice = price.switchIfEmpty(
    Mono.error { IllegalStateException("missing price") })                   // empty is an error

The demo runs both, on the discount:

with defaultIfEmpty: [24.00,3.50,0.00]
  price lookup cancelled
with switchIfEmpty: missing discount

Mono.zip turns one empty source into an empty result. Say what empty means on every source.

One more consequence: a Mono<Void> is always empty, so it can never take part in a zip. The last section shows the tool for that.

zip waits for one item from each belt. The next two operators either don't wait at all, or wait for a whole belt.

code.title: ZipDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; /** zip pairs by position. Mono.zip with an empty source completes empty, and cancels the others. */ public class ZipDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("Flux.zip: " + Flux.zip(Flux.just(1, 2, 3), Flux.just("a", "b")).collectList().block()); Mono<String> price = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(200)).thenReturn("24.00") .doOnCancel(() -> System.out.println(" price lookup cancelled")); Mono<String> deliveryFee = Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(100)).thenReturn("3.50"); Mono<String> discount = Mono.empty(); // this customer has no discount Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount) .doOnSuccess(t -> System.out.println("Mono.zip result: " + t)) // null means "completed empty" .block(); Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.defaultIfEmpty("0.00")) .doOnSuccess(t -> System.out.println("with defaultIfEmpty: " + t)) .block(); try { Mono.zip(price, deliveryFee, discount.switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalStateException("missing discount")))) .block(); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("with switchIfEmpty: " + e.getMessage()); } } }

try.expect: Flux.zip: [[1,a], [2,b]]. The plain Mono.zip prints price lookup cancelled and Mono.zip result: null: doOnSuccess got no value, because the zip completed empty. defaultIfEmpty gives [24.00,3.50,0.00] after about 200 ms, the time of the slowest lookup. switchIfEmpty cancels the price lookup again and prints with switchIfEmpty: missing discount, so now the problem is visible. With a real discount, every zip gets all three values after about 200 ms. The last one then prints nothing, because it only prints when it catches an error.

sections.h: Mix or take turns: merge and concat
sections.html:
Flux.merge(a, b) subscribes to every source at once and passes items on as they arrive, from whichever source has one. On the bakery line, it's two belts feeding one: loaves join in the order they arrive. It completes when all sources have completed, and by default the first error from any source ends it and cancels the rest.

Flux.concat(a, b) subscribes to b only after a has completed. The output is all of a, then all of b: the first belt runs until its end-of-day bell rings, and only then is the second switched on. That makes concat the right tool when the second source must not start early: orders already collected before the slow search for those still waiting, saved results before fresh ones, the first page before the rest.

The bakery's kitchen has a screen that shows new orders from two places, the shop counter and the website. At closing time it prints a day sheet. Here are both:

Java
Flux<String> screen = Flux.merge(counterOrders, webOrders);    // both at once, as they arrive
Flux<String> daySheet = Flux.concat(collected, waiting);       // waiting only after collected completes
Kotlin
val screen: Flux<String> = Flux.merge(counterOrders, webOrders)    // both at once, as they arrive
val daySheet: Flux<String> = Flux.concat(collected, waiting)       // waiting only after collected completes

The trap with concat is a first source that never completes. A live stream of counter orders never sends onComplete, so Flux.concat(counterOrders, webOrders) never subscribes to the web orders at all. They wait for a bell that never rings. If the inputs are endless, you want merge.

Flux.mergeSequential(a, b) sits in between. It subscribes to all its sources at once, like merge, but emits them source by source, like concat, and buffers what arrives early. It's the combining twin of flatMapSequential from the last lesson.

MergeConcatDemo, in the Try it, makes counter orders every 30 ms and web orders every 40 ms, three of each, and prints when each source is subscribed. One run on this busy machine:

merge:
  [  8 ms] counter subscribed
  [ 11 ms] web subscribed
  [counter-0, web-0, counter-1, web-1, counter-2, web-2], done at about 130 ms
concat:
  [  0 ms] counter subscribed
  [ 92 ms] web subscribed
  [counter-0, counter-1, counter-2, web-0, web-1, web-2], done at about 210 ms
mergeSequential:
  [  3 ms] counter subscribed
  [  3 ms] web subscribed
  [counter-0, counter-1, counter-2, web-0, web-1, web-2], done at about 120 ms

merge subscribed to both at once and mixed them by time. concat subscribed to the web orders only at 92 ms, when the counter source completed. It finished late, because the web source starts its own 40 ms clock only when it is subscribed. mergeSequential gave concat's order at merge's speed. It received web-0 and web-1 early, held them while the counter orders went out, and released both the moment the counter source completed. The figure below draws all three on one clock.

concat waits for each source to complete. Behind an endless source, the next one never starts.

merge and concat pass items through unchanged. Sometimes you want a new value, made from the latest item on each belt.

code.title: MergeConcatDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.function.BiFunction; /** Two order sources: the shop counter every 30 ms, the website every 40 ms. Three ways to combine them. */ public class MergeConcatDemo { static Flux<String> counter() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(30)).map(i -> "counter-" + i).take(3) .doOnSubscribe(s -> System.out.printf(" [%3d ms] counter subscribed%n", ms())); } static Flux<String> web() { return Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(40)).map(i -> "web-" + i).take(3) .doOnSubscribe(s -> System.out.printf(" [%3d ms] web subscribed%n", ms())); } static long t0; static long ms() { return (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; } public static void main(String[] args) { // warm up, so the first timing doesn't include class loading Flux.merge(Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(1)).take(2), Flux.just(9L)).concatWith(Flux.mergeSequential(Flux.just(1L))).blockLast(); String.format("%3d", 0); run("merge", Flux::merge); run("concat", Flux::concat); run("mergeSequential", Flux::mergeSequential); } static void run(String name, BiFunction<Flux<String>, Flux<String>, Flux<String>> combine) { System.out.println(name + ":"); t0 = System.nanoTime(); var out = combine.apply(counter(), web()).collectList().block(); System.out.printf(" %s, done at about %d ms%n", out, Math.round(ms() / 10.0) * 10); } }

try.expect: merge subscribes to both at once and mixes them: counter-0, web-0, counter-1, web-1, counter-2, web-2, done at about 120 to 140 ms. concat subscribes to the web source only at about 90 ms and finishes at about 210 ms. mergeSequential subscribes to both at once, emits the counter orders and then the web orders, and finishes at about 120 ms, like merge. Timings drift by a few milliseconds, more on a busy machine. With an endless counter source, concat prints counter subscribed and then nothing, forever: web subscribed never appears.

sections.html:
Flux.combineLatest(a, b, f) waits until every source has emitted at least once. After that, each new item from any source is combined with the most recent item from each of the others. Its Javadoc warns that elements "can and will be passed to the combinator multiple times", because the latest value stays in use until it is replaced.

On the bakery wall, it's the price board. The board shows a cake's price, its weight times the price per kilogram. The customer can change the weight on the order page, the owner can change the price per kilogram, and the board shows a new total whenever either one changes:

Java
Flux<BigDecimal> shown = Flux.combineLatest(weightsInKg, pricesPerKg, BigDecimal::multiply);
Flux<Bill> bills = orders.withLatestFrom(pricesPerKg, Order::billAt);      // only orders trigger
Kotlin
val shown: Flux<BigDecimal> = Flux.combineLatest(weightsInKg, pricesPerKg) { w, p -> w.multiply(p) }
val bills: Flux<Bill> = orders.withLatestFrom(pricesPerKg) { o, p -> o.billAt(p) }   // only orders trigger

CombineLatestDemo, in the Try it, runs zip and combineLatest on the same timeline. The weight is 1.5 kg at 0 ms and 2.0 kg at 300 ms. The price per kilogram is 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms and 21.00 at 400 ms:

zip:           [30.000, 44.000]
combineLatest: [30.000, 33.000, 44.000, 42.000]

zip paired by position, as gift boxes do: the first weight with the first price, and the second weight with the second price. So 2.0 kg was multiplied by 22.00, though the price had moved to 21.00 by the end, and the change at 200 ms never showed. combineLatest showed every state the inputs passed through: 1.5 x 20.00, then 1.5 x 22.00, then 2.0 x 22.00, then 2.0 x 21.00. That's what a price board should do. (The three decimal places come from BigDecimal, which keeps every digit when it multiplies a number with one decimal place by a number with two.)

Two details. combineLatest stays silent until every source has emitted once, so an input that might never emit needs a starting value, such as pricesPerKg.startWith(listPrice). And when only one side should trigger output, use withLatestFrom, from the second line above. Each order is billed at the price that is current when the order arrives, and a price change on its own emits nothing.

combineLatest shows every change. zip shows only matched pairs.

We now have four combinators and a few look-alikes. The last section puts them side by side, and looks at what happens when one source fails.

code.title: CombineLatestDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.reactive.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.math.BigDecimal; import java.time.Duration; /** A cake's weight and the price per kilogram change at different times. zip vs combineLatest. */ public class CombineLatestDemo { static Flux<BigDecimal> weights() { // 1.5 kg at 0 ms, 2.0 kg at 300 ms return Flux.concat(Mono.just(new BigDecimal("1.5")), Mono.just(new BigDecimal("2.0")).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(300))); } static Flux<BigDecimal> pricesPerKg() { // 20.00 at 100 ms, 22.00 at 200 ms, 21.00 at 400 ms return Flux.just("20.00", "22.00", "21.00").map(BigDecimal::new) .zipWith(Flux.just(100L, 100L, 200L), (price, wait) -> Mono.just(price).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(wait))) .concatMap(m -> m); } public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("zip: " + Flux.zip(weights(), pricesPerKg(), BigDecimal::multiply).collectList().block()); System.out.println("combineLatest: " + Flux.combineLatest(weights(), pricesPerKg(), BigDecimal::multiply).collectList().block()); } }

try.expect: zip: [30.000, 44.000] and combineLatest: [30.000, 33.000, 44.000, 42.000]. With withLatestFrom, only the weights trigger output. The first weight arrives at 0 ms, before any price exists, so it is dropped. The second weight (300 ms) uses the latest price, 22.00, which gives [44.000].

sections.h: Choosing a combinator, and what errors do
sections.html:
Most combining questions come down to this table:

You want Use
One result from several independent lookups Mono.zip, with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty on each source
Items from several streams, as they arrive Flux.merge
One stream after another, the next one started late Flux.concat
Several streams started together, output stream by stream Flux.mergeSequential
Item-by-item pairs Flux.zip
A value recomputed from the latest of every input Flux.combineLatest
Each item of one stream, with the latest of another withLatestFrom
Wait for several jobs that return Mono<Void> Mono.when
The first of several sources to produce a value Mono.firstWithValue

Mono.when(a, b) exists because Mono.zip and Mono<Void> don't mix: a Mono<Void> always completes empty, so zipping it completes the whole zip empty. Mono.when(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order)).then(Mono.just(ticket)) waits for both jobs to finish, then carries on with the ticket.

Mono.firstWithValue(millA.flourPrice(), millB.flourPrice()) asks two flour mills for a price, takes the first answer that arrives, and cancels the slower call. Empty sources are skipped. This is called a hedged request. It trades extra work for the mills for a faster answer, so keep it for calls that are cheap for the other side.

Every combinator in the table gives up at the first error: the first failure cancels the other sources. Each has a DelayError version, such as Mono.zipDelayError, Flux.mergeDelayError and Flux.concatDelayError, that lets the other sources finish and reports the error at the end. Use those when partial work is still useful, such as a nightly job that should process every file before it reports the bad one. The DelayError versions treat empty differently too: Mono.zipDelayError waits for the other sources to finish before it completes empty, instead of cancelling them.

The first error ends every combinator here. Use a DelayError version when the rest is still worth finishing.

If a combinator surprises you, ask the two questions from the start of this lesson. When does it subscribe to each source? And what does it do when a source completes early or empty? Those two answers explain every row of the table.

Quick check: Mono.zip(orderBook.save(order), prices.forCake(cake)), where the save is a Mono<Void> that completes after 20 ms and the price takes 100 ms. What does the zip emit, when, and what happens to the price lookup? (It completes empty at about 20 ms, because the save completed with no value, and it cancels the price lookup that is still in flight. A run here printed null at 22 ms. orderBook.save(order).then(prices.forCake(cake)) gives you the price after the save.)

compare.title: Fan-out with Mono.zip and Mono.when in Java and Kotlin

java.title: OrderPage.java
java.html: // three lookups at once; ready when the slowest one is Mono<Quote> quote = Mono.zip( prices.forCake(cake).switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), delivery.feeTo(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), tax.rateFor(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); // three jobs that return Mono<Void>: zip would complete empty Mono<String> done = Mono.when(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order), screen.show(order)) .then(Mono.just(ticket));

kotlin.title: OrderPage.kt
kotlin.html: // three lookups at once; ready when the slowest one is val quote: Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip( prices.forCake(cake).switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), delivery.feeTo(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), tax.rateFor(address).switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } // `when` is a Kotlin keyword, so the method name needs backticks val done: Mono<String> = Mono.`when`(orderBook.save(order), receipts.print(order), screen.show(order)) .then(Mono.just(ticket))

compare.note: The Reactor calls are the same. In Kotlin, tuple getters read as properties (t.t1), and core Reactor has no destructuring for tuples. when is a keyword in Kotlin, so Mono.when has to be written with backticks. Kotlin's own fan-out looks different: inside coroutineScope { } you start each call with async { } and then await() them. The Reactor bridge awaitSingleOrNull() turns an empty Mono into null, which the compiler then makes you handle. That makes the empty case hard to forget, while Mono.zip lets you forget it. The coroutines track covers async.

lab.title: Four combinators for the bakery's order page
steps: Read the Javadoc on the four methods in OrderPage. For each one, decide on the combinator before you write code: when must each source be subscribed, and when should output appear?
quote: run the three lookups at once, build a Quote, and turn an empty lookup into IllegalStateException("missing <name>").
kitchenScreen: counter and web orders, in the order they arrive.

daySheet: collected orders, then waiting ones, without subscribing to the waiting source early. The test checks this with a PublisherProbe, a test helper that records whether anything subscribed to it.
cakePrice: a new value whenever either the weight or the price per kilogram changes. Run the tests until all five pass.
hints: If the empty-quote test says expected: onError(); actual: onComplete(), you zipped the sources as they are. Add switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) to each one.
Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException(...)), with a supplier, builds the exception only if the source really is empty.
If cakePrice emits 30 and 44 but not 33, you used zip: it waits for a new item from both sides before it emits.

drill.title: Write the safe fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Mono<Quote> quote(Mono<BigDecimal> price, Mono<BigDecimal> deliveryFee, Mono<BigDecimal> taxRate) so that all three run at once, and any empty source fails with an IllegalStateException("missing ...") that names it. Then compare.

answer.html: Mono<Quote> quote(Mono<BigDecimal> price, Mono<BigDecimal> deliveryFee, Mono<BigDecimal> taxRate) { return Mono.zip( price.switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), deliveryFee.switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), taxRate.switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map(t -> new Quote(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())); } static <T> Mono<T> missing(String what) { return Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException("missing " + what)); }

alt.html: fun quote(price: Mono<BigDecimal>, deliveryFee: Mono<BigDecimal>, taxRate: Mono<BigDecimal>): Mono<Quote> = Mono.zip( price.switchIfEmpty(missing("price")), deliveryFee.switchIfEmpty(missing("delivery fee")), taxRate.switchIfEmpty(missing("tax rate"))) .map { t -> Quote(t.t1, t.t2, t.t3) } private fun <T : Any> missing(what: String): Mono<T> = Mono.error { IllegalStateException("missing $what") }

recap: Mono.zip subscribes to all its sources at once, so a fan-out takes as long as its slowest call.
If any zipped source completes empty, the zip completes empty and cancels the others. Say what empty means with switchIfEmpty or defaultIfEmpty.
merge subscribes to everything at once and emits in arrival order; concat subscribes to the next source only after the previous one completes.
concat behind an endless source never reaches the second source. Use merge for live feeds.
combineLatest emits again whenever any input changes, using the latest of the others. zip pairs strictly by position.
The limit: every combinator gives up at the first error and cancels the rest. The DelayError versions let the others finish, but none of them can try again.

explain.prompt: A teammate's order page uses Mono.zip over three lookups, and it "sometimes shows nothing, with no error". Explain in your own words what is happening, and how you would fix it so it can't happen silently again.
explain.answer: Mono.zip needs a value from every source. If any of them completes without a value, there is nothing to combine, so the zip completes empty at once and cancels the other lookups. No error is raised, so nothing is logged, and the page has nothing to show. It happens for whichever lookup can be empty, for example a delivery area with no tax rate set up. The fix is to decide what empty means for each lookup and write it down before zipping: switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(...)) where empty is a real error, and defaultIfEmpty(...) where there is a sensible default. Then add a test with an empty stub for each lookup, so the case stays covered.

deeper.html:
Zip in a chain. mono.zipWith(other) zips two Monos without the static call. Mono.zipWhen(value -> otherCall(value)) runs the second call after the first and gives you both results. That's handy when the second lookup needs the first one's answer, such as fetching a customer and then that customer's discount. It is one after another on purpose, so it takes the sum of both times.

Numbering items. flux.index() pairs each item with its position, which is often what people reach for zip with Flux.range to do.

Many Monos, number unknown. For a list of calls, Mono.zip(listOfMonos, array -> ...) exists, but it hands you an Object[]. Usually Flux.fromIterable(ids).flatMap(this::lookup, n).collectList() is clearer: it caps how many calls run at once, which Mono.zip cannot, and it returns results in arrival order (use flatMapSequential to keep the input order).

Merge and backpressure. merge asks each source for a small batch ahead (a prefetch) and requests more only as items move downstream, so a fast source can't flood a slow subscriber. Lesson 7 of this track looks at demand in detail.

switchIfEmpty is lazy, its argument isn't. switchIfEmpty(Mono.error(new IllegalStateException(...))) builds the exception object on every call, even when the source has a value. That's cheap but wasteful, and the stack trace points at the place where the chain was built. The supplier form, Mono.error(() -> new IllegalStateException(...)), builds it only when it is needed.
